newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan to meet despite crisis in Delhi.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan to meet despite crisis in Delhi.

text.p: India and Pakistan will hold peace talks next week in New Delhi despite the political crisis threatening Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said on Friday.
Gujral told Reuters he would meet his Pakistani counterpart, Gohar Ayub Khan, during and after a meeting of foreign ministers of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), set for April 7-8.
Foreign secretaries of the two countries held four days of talks that broke a three-year stalemate and ended on a positive note last Monday when they agreed to hold a subsequent round in Islamabad.
But they were unable to set dates for the next meeting, partly because of the political turmoil in New Delhi, where Deve Gowda faces a vote of confidence in parliament on April 11.

On Tuesday, Khan said that talks next week with Gujral might be put off because of the looming trust vote. Gujral said on the same day that it would be understandable if the talks did not go ahead as planned.

But the two sides have since decided to go ahead with the negotiations in spite of the political uncertainty, which has appeared to wane as the possibility of a patch-up between Deve Gowda's ruling coalition and the rival Congress party emerges.
Asked if he would meet his Pakistani counterpart next week, Gujral said: "Yes, I am looking forward to it, and I'm sure when he comes here we'll have the opportunity of getting together."
Gujral, who spoke after addressing senior NAM officials, said he and Khan would hold talks on the sidelines of next week's NAM ministerial meeting and also after the conference.
He was asked if the two ministers would be able to discuss substantive issues despite the political upheaval in New Delhi.
"I believe that we will meet as friends to exchange notes. We both are democracies. We understand sometimes democratic systems do come under strain," he said.

Gujral was asked if he and Khan would prepare an agenda for a meeting of the two nations' prime ministers in the Maldives in May on the sidelines of a summit of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).
"Yes, definitely because primarily you must keep in mind that governments are ongoing institutions. Whichever government is in office, we will definitely pay attention to this," he said.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947, two of them over the disputed Himalayan region of Kashmir.

The previous round of high-level bilateral talks that ended in January 1994 bogged down in disagreement over Kashmir, where Indian security forces have been fighting a separatist insurgency since 1990.
After Nawaz Sharif was elected as Pakistan's prime minister in February, the two countries agreed to resume peace talks.
During their four days of talks that ended on Monday, the foreign secretaries discussed a wide range of issues and focused on setting procedures for subsequent rounds.
Pakistan has insisted that the two sides address differences over Kashmir. India has said it is willing to reach agreements in other areas before settling the thorny Kashmir dispute.
